# Agent 3: an LLM

One `responses.create` call per problem. No tools, no retries on a wrong answer,
no few-shot examples, no conversation, no per-problem-set tuning.

## Exactly what gets sent

Both: **the assembled sheet *and* every panel individually.** For a 3×3 problem
that is **37 content blocks — 20 pieces of text and 17 images** in one request.

![What one API call contains](../docs/llm_payload.png)

*Generated by `scripts/make_payload_figure.py`, which walks the real
`build_input()` output, so the picture cannot drift from the code.*

The order matters and is deliberate:

| # | Block | Why it is there |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Text: the grid layout (`A B C / D E F / G H ?`), how many options there are | The model needs to know the geometry; the sheet alone does not say which cell is "G" |
| 2 | **Image: the whole problem sheet** (1280×1024) | Spatial arrangement, the way a person sees it. Rows and columns are only visible here |
| 3 | Text: "Now each panel on its own. Matrix cells:" | Marks the switch from overview to detail |
| 4–19 | **`Cell A:` + image**, … through `Cell H:` (184×184 each) | Individual panels at full resolution, each labelled, so the model can refer to one precisely |
| 20 | Text: "Answer options:" | |
| 21–36 | **`Option 1:` + image**, … through `Option 8:` | Same treatment for the candidates |
| 37 | Text: "Which option (1-8) completes the matrix?" | |

Sending both views is the point. The sheet carries the *structure* — which
panels form a row, which cell is missing — and a downscaled thumbnail of one
cell inside it is far too small to compare shapes reliably. The individual
panels carry the *detail* but lose all spatial relationship. Neither alone is
enough.

**No verbal representation is ever sent.** Two of the eight sets ship with a
text description of each figure; the other six do not, so it is withheld from
every agent to keep the sets comparable. The LLM gets pixels, exactly like the
other two agents.

## The prompt

The complete system prompt — 134 words, the only domain knowledge the model is
given:

```
You are solving Raven's Progressive Matrices, a nonverbal reasoning test.

You are shown a matrix of figures with the last cell missing, then a numbered
list of answer options. Work out the rule (or combination of rules) that
governs how the figures change across the rows and down the columns, then
choose the option that completes the matrix.

Rules in these problems include: shapes being reflected, rotated or resized;
objects being added, removed, filled or unfilled; a property changing by a
constant amount along a row or column; the third cell being the pixel union,
intersection or difference of the first two; and Latin-square arrangements
where every row and column contains each shape exactly once.

Check your candidate answer against BOTH the rows and the columns before
committing. Answer with the option number only.
```

That last paragraph — listing the rule families — is the one piece of help the
model gets, and it is the same list the classical agent in `02_classical_ai/`
implements by hand. The difference is that the classical agent had to be *told
how to test* each of those rules in code; the LLM is only told they exist.

## The reply

Constrained by a JSON schema so the answer is always a parseable integer:

```json
{"rule": "<one sentence>", "answer": <int>, "confidence": <0-1>}
```

The `rule` field is recorded in the results CSV for every problem, including the
ones it gets wrong — it is worth reading as the model's own account of what it
thought the pattern was.

## Tokens are not a neutral unit

Every model receives the identical 17 images, and what each one charges for them
varies by nearly 7×: `gpt-5.6-sol` counts 2,540 input tokens per problem,
`gemini-3.1-pro` counts 17,047. Compare models on **cost**, never on tokens.

## Running it

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...
python 03_llm/solver.py --model gpt-5.6-sol              # all 96
python 03_llm/solver.py --model gpt-5.6-sol --per-set 2  # 16-problem smoke test

# other labs, same payload, via OpenRouter (key in ~/.openrouter_key)
python 03_llm/openrouter_solver.py --all
```

Results land in `../results/llm_<model>_answers.csv` plus a `_summary.txt`.

## Model choice

`gpt-5.6` ships as three variants. A pilot on the two hardest sets (Challenge D
and Challenge E, 24 problems) put `luna` and `sol` level at 23/24, but `sol`
used about a quarter of `luna`'s reasoning tokens and half the wall clock, so
`sol` is the primary model. Other labs are compared in
[`../EPILOGUE.md`](../EPILOGUE.md).

## Two caveats worth stating plainly

**Contamination.** These puzzles have been in a public GitHub repository since
2017, and Raven's-style matrices are widely discussed online. There is no way to
rule out that some of this is in the training data. The score is a score on a
public benchmark, not a clean measurement of novel visual reasoning.

**A "no answer" is usually your bug.** An unparseable reply scores zero, and the
first pass of the epilogue produced three false 0/96 results: an 8,000-token
output budget let reasoning models spend the whole allowance thinking and return
an empty message, `gpt-4-turbo` rejects any budget above 4,096, and o-series
models reject the `max_tokens` parameter outright. Fixing the harness took o3
from 72/96 to 76/96. Assume a suspiciously round zero is yours before it is
theirs.
